title: NSF’s X-Labs Program Draws Support From Charities and Investors
raw_summary: When the U.S. National Science Foundation began its X-Labs program in May, the agency said the higher-risk, higher-funded awards would create new kinds of partnerships that would confront urgent scientific and technological challenges. Now the NSF is doubling down on the idea, with an announcement in October that charities, companies, and investment funds would provide X-Lab winners practical support such as laboratory space, software, shared equipment, and access to key data and expert guidance. The help provided by these organizations, which the NSF is calling “ consortium partners ,” will not give them ownership stakes in the X-Labs projects. The addition of the consortium partners may help the initial winners—who will be announced later in November or December and receive US $1.5 million for a 9-month planning phase—reach the aggressive targets needed to compete for much larger $50 million multiyear grants. “It’s a way of telling X-Labs applicants you don’t need to reinvent the wheel, so you’re not spending half of your X-Labs money to go build or buy basic infrastructure,” says Matt Cimaglia , an investor in consortium partners Occam Foundry and Florida Quantum Center . NSF X-Labs Focus on AI, Computing, and More The NSF initially announced two focus areas for the X-Labs program: scientific instruments for sensing and imaging and photonic microchips for quantum systems . In September, the agency followed up with three additional areas in AI for physical devices , decoding biological sequences , and pushing the physical limits of computing . The NSF requires potential X-Labs award recipients to eventually demonstrate autonomy : Leaders for projects must be focused on the work full-time, for example, and must be able to make hiring and spending decisions independently from any university or commercial owners. That agility sets X-Labs apart, along with the risk appetite. Consortium partners saw the potential to provide infrastructure and operations support to allow X-Labs recipients to focus on research. “[We’re] very interested in the enabling structures of R&D,” says Joshua M. Greenberg , program director at the Sloan Foundation, one of the participating partners. Greenberg says that the foundation has supported multiple focused research organizations, or FROs, already. FROs are independent entities in the same vein as what the X-Labs program hopes to create. Unlike university laboratories or larger tech companies, FROs are founded with a time-limited purpose of advancing research in a well-defined area. Because they start with a clean slate, FROs may lack the infrastructure that university or corporate research groups might inherit. To address that lack of infrastructure, bioengineering service firm Ginkgo Bioworks , in Boston, is offering X-Lab winners up to $5 million worth of access to its “cloud lab,” says Jason Kelly , the firm’s CEO and founder. Ginkgo’s cloud lab can conduct complex and flexible laboratory work, and the company will also offer laboratory space and internal datasets that could be useful for training AI models. Kelly is enthusiastic about the potential for X-Labs, which he says have the potential to “pull platforms into existence” like the federal Human Genome Project once did, which enabled a lot of subsequent innovation. As scientific and technology companies become more powerful, Kelly says, it’s natural that governments should revisit how to involve them in government-led science. “The scale of companies is not like it was in the Vannevar Bush era [in the 1940s],” he says, “so how should the United States leverage those [much larger, more capable] companies? It’s silly to leave them on the sidelines.” In 1945, Vannevar Bush wrote an influential report that helped shape the modern NSF and U.S. federal science funding. A July report by Michael Kratsios, director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, offered the current administration’s vision for an update to the Bush report, including the role of X-Labs. Arthur Daemmrich , a historian of U.S. technology policy at Arizona State University (ASU), says he welcomes the administration’s willingness to experiment with science funding. “The field had gotten very staid…this administration has a certain energy that I haven’t seen in past administrations.” He also points out that the X-Labs approach to scientific work is “like gig work for science,” so while it may work for some people and some problems, it may not work for others. The contribution these larger projects make to society is also worth studying, says Zachary Pirtle , a former NASA program manager and now a colleague of Daemmrich’s at ASU, though it’s an open question just how to do so. “If you’re funding these amazing teams and you want them to benefit society, you can’t just have engineers and scientists. Do you need to have economists on some of these teams? Or a variety of different social scientists?” Academics Embrace X-Labs AI Model Some academics are leaning into the X-Labs model. Nathalie Risso , an electrical engineer at the University of Arizona in Tucson, does applied research on automating mining equipment. Risso is applying under the AI for physical systems topic, aiming to test self-learning AI operation of heavy mining equipment. “X-Labs lets us explore things that are bigger than we can do in a lab, or that we might have done in a mine, but they won’t let us use their concentrators because they cost so much,” she says. The costs of getting it right exceed a typical university grant and the cost of getting it wrong is more than any industry partner wants to risk. These kinds of missed opportunities justify an X-Labs–size program, say supporters. A spokesperson for the Secunda Family Foundation, another X-Labs consortium partner, says that AI is part of what makes the NSF’s approach so urgent. “AI and other new technologies are rapidly changing what scientists can attempt, but the infrastructure and institutions supporting research have to evolve with them.” “Engineers should be excited about the fact that there are open and new opportunities for people with an entrepreneurial mindset,” Cimaglia says. “You don’t have to be part of a university.” Greenberg agrees. “This is more like founding a new organization than pitching a specific research project.”

title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability. Does true zero-trust architecture exist? The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist? Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. title: Europe’s Digital Wallets May Be More Traceable Than Intended
raw_summary: Millions of European Union citizens should soon have access to digital wallets , as member states roll out their implementations of the European Digital Identity Regulation ahead of an end-of-the-year deadline. But the digital-identity wallets, which are intended to provide a secure and private place to store identifying information such as bank-account information, diplomas, and government IDs, such as driver’s licenses, could leave behind a trail of cryptographic clues that makes it possible to recognize someone across services. Cryptographers warn that the technology protecting individual privacy may not yet go far enough to stop people from being tracked. Advances in cryptographic techniques since the law was passed in 2024 means this problem could be solved. However, the law doesn’t require that these techniques be used, and cryptographers that IEEE Spectrum spoke with are split as to whether the wallets should be rolled out at all without such a requirement in place, and whether they’ll be secure enough without it. With digital wallets, when someone is asked to provide their ID, a digital, verifiable form of the ID can be transmitted, via a QR code for example. When scanned with a verification app, it would show basic identifying user information, according to Anna Lysyanskaya , a professor of computer science at Brown University. The EU’s digital-identity regulation already includes a requirement for selective disclosure, which allows people to share only the attributes requested by the person checking identification rather than handing over an entire document. A bar checking someone’s age, for example, could request a simple confirmation that a person is over 18 and not need their full name or address.. Tracking Risks in EU Digital Wallets When the person who requested the ID scans it, they still record some personal information, such as the digital signature and identifiers that are required to check the ID. This additional information can serve as a way of tracking a user even if the attributes shared are quite common. Two requesters could share this information to show they had interacted with the same person, says Johannes Schönrich , the director at the FIM Research Center for Information Management at the Augsburg Technical University of Applied Sciences, in Germany. If two parties can share that information, that would be a problem: EU legislation specifies that the wallets should also be unlinkable, which means that “tracking a user by means of [these] digital attestations should not be possible,” says Schönrich. One way to address the problem is to issue multiple versions of a user’s credentials, each with different cryptographic information attached, says Lysyanskaya. The wallet could keep track of which certificates have already been used, ensuring that a different one is presented during each interaction. “If you allow a service provider to say, Look, I’m not supporting the Google protocol, I want a traditional verification, you essentially allow the service provider to do a kind of downgrade.” —Jaap-Henk Hoepman, Radboud University This approach has limitations. If the issuer—the government department that creates and digitally verifies that the credential is authentic—can identify who a credential was originally issued to, it could potentially help link the different versions back to the same person, according to Lysyanskaya. “Now anybody you’ve ever interacted with has some kind of way of tracking you,” she says. “If this kind of interaction becomes really ubiquitous…then unless we place a tremendous amount of trust in both issuers and verifiers to guard our privacy, we may encounter a situation where everybody knows at all times what everybody else is up to, by just leaving these little digital crumbs of information about yourself.” Lysyanskaya was one of 16 cryptographers who were invited to provide feedback for the European Commission when the law was passed in 2024. They recommended using anonymous credentials, which use zero-knowledge proofs to let people demonstrate their identity or eligibility without revealing unnecessary personal information. How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Work Zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to convince another that something is true without needing to send any additional information beyond the fact that it is true. For example, they would allow someone to demonstrate that they hold a valid government-issued credential, or meet a particular requirement, without revealing the underlying personal information or creating the same linkable record of the interaction, says Lysyanskaya. If these two people, the person checking the ID and the person being asked for it ever meet again, there will be no record of any earlier encounters. The service provider could still verify that the credential is authentic, has not expired or been revoked, and has not been manipulated. However, it would receive less information than it does under traditional verification methods. “You learn exactly what you need, but not a single bit more about anything that might accidentally be disclosed but is not that necessary,” says Schönrich. Zero-knowledge proofs have existed in cryptography since the 1980s , but teams of researchers have only recently developed techniques to run them on more-constrained devices like smartphones. Shortly after the EU’s digital-wallet regulations were passed in 2024, for example, a research team at Google found a way to generate zero-knowledge proofs using credentials signed with the elliptic-curve digital-signature algorithm, which generates and authenticates digital signatures efficiently enough to be used in a digital wallet. Those kinds of credentials allow individuals to prove that a credential is valid without revealing the cryptographic signature that could otherwise make separate interactions linkable, according to Jaap-Henk Hoepman , an associate professor of computer science at Radboud University, in the Netherlands. The European Commission wants to conduct more research on implementing zero-knowledge proofs before making them a mandatory requirement for wallet operators from day 1. Because of that, it considers the proofs to be “a core road map item,” according to the universal digital blueprint for the wallets. EU governments are free to implement them on a by-country basis if they so choose. The Commission said on its GitHub page for the wallets that zero-knowledge proofs are not yet mandatory because “there is currently no clear, certifiable approach agreed at EU level,” and that it needs to do more pan-European consultation with cryptographers and groups, such as the European Cybersecurity Certification Group (ECCG), that oversee the profession. “Refinement at this stage focuses on establishing common understanding and boundaries, rather than immediate deployment to secure and privacy-preserving future integration,” the Commission’s GitHub post from June 2026 reads. Schönrich says he understands the Commission’s position, but wants them to commit to a binding timeline for introducing zero-knowledge proofs in the next few years for a second version of the wallets. title: The Race to Build a “Find My” for AI Chips
raw_summary: In a bid to limit China’s AI capabilities, the United States imposed restrictions in 2022 on the export of certain advanced chips to China. But throughout the AI boom those chips have kept turning up in China anyway . On 1 October 2026, the U.S. arrested a man on charges of sending over US $300 million worth of GPU-equipped servers to China using paperwork intended for shipments to Malaysia and Singapore . As chip smuggling and diversion continues, the United States is learning that the more it tries to limit the motion of its AI chips, the harder they are to precisely locate . To help curb the issue, the U.S. is turning to location verification. Last March, the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee passed a bill requiring location verification for advanced AI chips. Ahead of the U.S.-China summit in late September, legislators called for a floor vote on that and related bills. If such a requirement were to pass, how would chipmakers comply? They could build tamper-proof root-of-trust hardware, implement cryptographic signing and transmission, or possibly even fingerprint individual chips. These strategies could function as a way to keep track of where AI chips actually are in the world, much like how the popular “Find My” feature can locate misplaced Apple devices. Pings that pinpoint positions Location verification can take different forms, such as geolocation mechanisms, inventory-management tools, mail-in inspections, and video inspections. A combination of approaches, such as ping-based location verification (PLV) supplemented by physical inspections, would be a feasible and robust approach, say the authors of a September Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) report on chip-location tracking. To deduce an AI chip’s location, PLV measures the time it takes for a ping to travel from the chip to multiple trusted “landmark” servers around the world and back. Kyle Miller , a senior research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report, says that for new AI chips, manufacturers could integrate PLV functionality into the hardware itself, while a firmware update could be applied to chips already in circulation. Not all AI chips should be tracked, the researchers note. “The priority should be for the highest-end data-center chips—the cream of the crop in high-end data-center GPUs,” says Jacob Feldgoise , a senior data-research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report. A similar initiative involves transmitting encrypted “ sovereignty certificates .” These certificates act as “cryptographic credentials that provide verifiable, unforgeable proof of the physical location of a computing device, such as a CPU or GPU, at a specific point in time,” per the draft specification published by secure computing firm Lucid Computing . “If you can use a private key that exists on a particular chip, and you can sign a message with that cryptographic key, and then that message is received by a so-called landmark server, then you can send a couple of those messages and time those messages. A lot of modern chips come with trusted execution environments that support a hardware root of trust where you can sign these messages,” says Kristian Rönn , CEO and cofounder of Lucid Computing. “You get a radius of where the chip has to be.” PLV could have some effect on chip smugglers, Miller says. “They know if they turn this chip on, it’s going to start pinging these landmark servers. That could deter some smuggling.” And when the system flags a chip as residing in a unintended location, “the PLV data gives you a better sense of when and where it was moved,” he adds. However, ping-based location verification can only uncover diversion after it has happened. It can’t track offline chips that are in storage, in transit, or have yet to be activated. And when a chip fails to respond to a ping request, the system won’t know whether it’s due to a valid reason or nefarious causes. This is where physical inspections come in. “You need to do that follow-on investigative work. You need to physically go to these data centers and do those physical audits as well. Essentially, [PLV] generates leads, and you track down those leads,” says Miller. A PLV system involves sending signals from a chip to and from trusted servers and measuring the travel time. Source image: CSET A “lie detector” for data centers Despite the safeguards around ping-based location verification, the methodology remains vulnerable to particular attacks. If adversaries gain physical access to a chip, for example, they could prevent it from sending signals, or they could extract cryptographic keys and spoof a signal from the intended location. To fight that, some security researchers are exploring hardware fingerprints instead of cryptographic keys. One study demonstrated a proof-of-concept GPU fingerprinting function that produced unique fingerprints for Nvidia H200 GPUs based on their manufacturing variations and random numbers as seeds. “You want to support other types of fingerprinting because not all chips have a hardware root of trust. You might want to use some statistical fingerprinting to know that the chip is what it’s supposed to be,” Rönn says. “It also requires good physical security around the chips, such as tamper-proofing. Over time, you ideally want to have more defense in depth.” Additionally, the CSET report warns that PLV is costly. And if China achieves the ability to craft its own advanced AI chips, “then tracking the export of U.S. chips is less of a strategic priority,” says Miller. Hanna Dohmen , a senior research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report, points to other gaps in the U.S. export-control regime. “Currently, Chinese companies are legally able to remotely access AI chips abroad through cloud-service providers,” she says. These advanced AI chips might be installed in data centers across Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia, which are increasingly serving Chinese firms . Whether or not a “Find My” for AI chips becomes a regulatory requirement, Feldgoise envisions tighter conditions for the export of advanced AI chips. “This is based on the increasing importance of compute to national and economic security,” he says. “The chips that generate compute are being seen as a strategic resource, so I would be unsurprised if the due diligence requirements on these devices increase as time passes.” Rönn views sovereignty certificates as essential tools in the future, likening it to a “lie detector” for data centers that answers the “where, how, what, and who questions for us to know that they comply with a basic standard of security when it comes to AI systems.”

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
raw_summary: When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits. Last year, we shipped just that , with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it. More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged. The first is automation : Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines. The second is agents and harnesses : Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too. As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance. Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three. More secure workflows The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection. Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end , before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools. Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change: Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log. Encryption on self-hosted Worlds Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams. A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management . Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay: More security work in v5 Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads. You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0 , inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability. A redesigned trace viewer The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development. Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets. Workflows in every region In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1 . Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress. For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region . Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path. By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration: To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start() . That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay: The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1 . Infrastructure reliability Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover. With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors. As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug. Agent-ready performance In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today. Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit. In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes. The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures. Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers: Fewer queue hops In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout. The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms . Incremental replay Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log : replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms . The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes. WebSocket streaming Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default . In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds . Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression. These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application. title: "Eppur si muove": Convergence Within and Between Countries
raw_summary: Kremer, Willis, and You (2022) report that over six decades richer countries lost their growth advantage. Acemoglu and Molina (2022) and Pesaran and Smith (2026) reply that such regressions cannot measure catch-up when countries head toward different moving destinations.

title: The gig economy and digital payments
raw_summary: The growth of the “gig” economy could have far-reaching implications for payment systems. Gig work involves digital platforms that intermediate between workers and (retail or business) customers, in areas as diverse as ride-hailing and food delivery, freelance design and professional services, and customer service.

title: Ready-to-run global liquidity stress tests for banks and banking systems
raw_summary: Liquidity risk remains a persistent threat to financial stability, as starkly demonstrated by the 2023 banking turmoil in the United States and Europe. Hence, the ability to quickly gauge banks’ liquidity risks could prove useful especially during periods of market stress, but also to assess differences in liquidity buffers across peer economies and banks.

title: US monetary policy, macroeconomic news and the global secular decline of interest rates
raw_summary: The global secular decline in long-term interest rates since the 1990s has been largely driven by cumulative yield changes during U.S. monetary policy announcement windows (FOMC windows).

title: Gaining (and losing) currency: a global database of currencies, 1850-2026
raw_summary: Over the past two centuries, officially issued currencies have become firmly en trenched as a nearly universal institution in economies around the world. But the path to this arrangement has not been smooth: currencies have come and gone, in line with political changes, periods of hyperinflation or currency reforms and, in some cases, entry into currency unions.

title: Scenarios for future banking: implications for profitability, liquidity and solvency
raw_summary: Who will perform banking’s core functions a decade from now, and how will risks and profitability evolve? Our framework structures expert judgement rather than forecasts.

title: Prewar US business cycles under uncertainty: reconstructing quarterly GDP before 1947
raw_summary: Official quarterly US GDP estimates begin in 1947; earlier quarterly histories must be reconstructed using annual benchmarks and historical indicators. To investigate uncertainty in these reconstructions, this paper systematically compares specifications drawn from the literature for reconstructing quarterly GDP during 1919–1946. The comparison evaluates predictions on concealed postwar quarters and separates variation across specifications from coefficient uncertainty within a model.

title: Refined slippage: variance reduction using counterfactual returns
raw_summary: A new metric is introduced that benchmarks fill prices against counterfactual prices, rather than the arrival price

title: Smile dynamics and rough volatility

title: Banking System Vulnerability: 2026 Update
raw_summary: As in previous years, we provide in this post an update on the vulnerability of the U.S. banking system based on four analytical models that capture different aspects of this vulnerability. We use data through 2026:Q2 to update our analysis and discuss how the vulnerability measures have changed since our last update one year ago .

title: A Look at the Wider Divide in Credit Card Delinquency by Income
raw_summary: Credit card delinquency rose sharply between 2022 and 2024, and the increase was steepest among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods. Here, we check in on credit card performance by neighborhood income and trace when the borrowers who are now struggling with their payments were issued cards. We find that during the pandemic, an increasing share of new credit cards went to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress.

title: Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150‑Year Perspective
raw_summary: Has U.S. monetary policy actually improved over time? Or was the apparent success of the modern Federal Reserve mostly the result of more favorable economic conditions and better luck? In this post, we summarize our paper , * which develops a framework for comparing monetary policy across different economic environments. Our approach asks how close policy came to the best response given the economic conditions and shocks policymakers faced. Applying this framework to 150 years of U.S. monetary history, we find that meaningful improvements in monetary policy occurred only in the last thirty years. Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.

title: The U.S. Oil Sector’s Role in Restraining Prices
raw_summary: The start of the Middle East conflict in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply. In response, oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels. The U.S. oil sector was a key factor in moderating the shock. For one, its steady increases in drilling helped create a large oversupply in the global market before the conflict, making it less of a challenge to offset the drop in Middle East oil output. In addition, U.S. commercial and government inventories were rapidly drawn down, filling half the gap between global supply and demand in the second quarter by some estimates. Inventories, though, are a limited resource and U.S. stockpiles stopped falling in July. As a consequence, the continued shortfall in global production has been managed by running down inventories in the rest of the world.

title: How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates
raw_summary: Why is it that two borrowers who look much alike can be offered very different rates when applying for a credit card? In a recent paper , we address this question by examining how the rate offered changes when the lender’s funding cost falls. Data on 14 million newly issued cards show that when a lender's funding costs decline, the lender passes less of that decline on to the offer rate when it holds a large market share. That is, two borrowers with similar credit scores and incomes borrowing from the same lender can see noticeably different interest rates on the credit card they are applying for.

title: How Do Banking Supervisors Deal with Failing Banks?
raw_summary: In this post, we discuss insights from a recent staff report on the role of banking supervision in identifying and disciplining failing banks. We show that bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity. Yet hard information is itself partly produced by supervision, as our evidence suggests that supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses. We argue that supervision faces a trade-off: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks, but it can also lead to tighter regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.

title: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence
raw_summary: Benjamin Guin Most discussion of AI in organisations focuses on productivity: as analysis becomes cheaper, decision-making should improve. This post argues that an important consequence lies elsewhere. Where the relevant information is accessible, a wider range of people can produce professionally presented analysis and submit it to decision-makers. Responsibility for decisions, however, remains concentrated and … Continue reading AI, accountability and the economics of evidence →

title: FEDS Paper: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
raw_summary: Nick Carollo , Leland D. Crane , Daniel Garcia Molina , and Joseph Nichols We assess the current evidence on how AI-related investment and the use of AI are affecting the U.S. macroeconomy. Specifically, we document the boom in data center capital investment, the current rate of adoption of AI tools in the economy, the impact of the AI-related investment surge on prices, and discuss whether AI tools have affected the labor market and productivity yet. Driven by current and expected future demand for AI services, investment in data centers, both the physical structures and semiconductor chips and other IT equipment inside the structures, has climbed sharply. AI adoption is growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all. AI model-producing firms have also grown extremely fast, and now account for a noticeable fraction of software industry gross output. Prices have climbed in sectors that provide direct inputs to the data centers, such as memory chips. Effects on the labor market so far appear small and somewhat mixed. Similarly, the effects of AI on aggregate productivity growth also appear to be small so far, and the recent pickup in productivity likely reflects factors that predated the diffusion on generative AI.

title: FEDS Paper: Costly Misdemeanours: Labour Market Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving Violations
raw_summary: Kabir Dasgupta , Marco Francesconi, Jonathan James Linda Kirkpatrick, and Alexander Plum This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market outcomes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after conviction to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.

title: FEDS Paper: Heterogeneity in Service Fee Sensitivity: Evidence from ATM Surcharges
raw_summary: Krzysztof Wozniak Service fees continue to proliferate in a wide range of markets, from retail to payments, generating questions about their impact on consumer choice, competition, and fairness. This paper explores how sensitivity to such fees varies across consumers, use cases, and competitive settings, and whether it is affected by consumer learning. I am able to conduct this in-depth empirical analysis thanks to a uniquely detailed, high-frequency panel data set on surcharged ATM cash withdrawals. Results show that average elasticity estimates mask substantial heterogeneity in consumer sensitivity to service fees. I explore ways in which market and behavioral mechanisms can help explain this heterogeneity. Finally, I investigate whether consumers strategically adjust their behavior in response to service fees.

title: Advancing safe agentic AI: ASKS symposium highlights
raw_summary: Highlights from UIUC’s 2026 ASKS Fall Symposium. On September 24–25, academic researchers, enterprise scientists and leaders gathered at the Thomas M. Siebel Center for Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) for the ASKS Fall Symposium. The event marked a major milestone in the partnership between Capital One and the University of Illinois through the Capital One Center for Generative AI Safety, Knowledge Systems and Cybersecurity (ASKS). Designed to advance the safety, reliability and security of generative AI models, the symposium featured keynotes, research readouts, panel debates and a hands-on AI red-teaming workshop. From models to agents: Navigating the age of action The symposium kicked off with opening remarks and a fireside chat titled “From models to agents: rethinking AI research, safety, and cybersecurity in the age of action.” Moderated by ASKS Co-Director Heng Ji, the session featured Prem Natarajan, chief scientist and chief enterprise AI officer at Capital One, alongside Nancy Amato, director of the Siebel School of Computing and Data Science. The discussion framed the fundamental transition taking place across the AI landscape: moving away from models that merely generate text to autonomous agentic AI-systems that can set goals, execute code, operate tools and take multistep actions. Natarajan highlighted Capital One’s “destination-back” scientific approach, emphasizing that in highly regulated spaces like financial services, autonomous agency requires rigorous safety mechanisms. As AI stops just “talking” and starts “acting,” industry-academic partnerships like ASKS become essential to build new sandboxing, auditing and accountability frameworks. Panel spotlight: Word models vs. world models One of the highlights of the day was a panel exploring the fundamental limits of current large language models: “ Word models vs. world models: Do LLMs understand the world-or just describe it? ” Moderated by Heng Ji, the panel brought together UIUC faculty members Gang Wang, Julia Hockenmaier, Chengxiang Zhai and Katie Driggs-Campbell alongside Capital One AI leaders Sambit Sahu and Yue (Rex) Wu. The panelists debated whether modern foundation models genuinely comprehend real-world dynamics or simply replicate statistical language patterns. The consensus pointed toward a need for multimodal visual grounding, physical intelligence and trace-aware reasoning to move models from passive text descriptions to true situation understanding. Pioneering research readouts Throughout the symposium, awarded faculty members and doctoral fellows presented breakthrough findings from ASKS-funded research projects spanning safety, code reasoning and cybersecurity: LLM reasoning and faithfulness: Hao Peng presented work on advancing reasoning faithfulness without explicit rewards, while Talia Ringer’s team introduced TrACE-Contrast for faithful code reasoning. Yuxiong Wang presented work on building safe and trustworthy LLM-based agents by addressing key challenges in evaluation, privacy preservation and multi-agent coordination. Guaranteed safety for agentic AI: Sasa Misailovic detailed SafeAgency , a framework designed to guarantee safety in agentic workflows, complemented by Katherine Driggs-Campbell’s analysis of failures in agentic systems. Security and cybersecurity benchmarks: Bo Li’s team showcased Sentinel Agent for secure agentic architectures, Varun Chandrasekaran’s team presented insights into pragmatic LLM jailbreaking and Daniel Kang introduced CVE-Bench++ , a benchmark for evaluating AI agents in cybersecurity contexts. Keynote on code generation safety: ASKS Director Gang Wang delivered a keynote on automated red-teaming and reasoning to secure code generation models. Doctoral fellow spotlights: Emerging researchers Hyeonjeong Ha, Jeonghwan Kim, Yizhuo Chen, Cheng Qian and Chenyuan Yang presented research on perceptual grounding, data sanitization and physical intelligence. The afternoon program highlighted Capital One’s research initiatives during a session chaired by Sambit Sahu, featuring lightning talks by senior research directors Kartik Balasubramaniam, Genta Winata and Stephen Rawls on scalable AI foundations and system architecture. Red-teaming workshop On the second day of the event, domain specialists convened for a smaller, more intimate AI red-teaming workshop. Alexandre Day (Capital One), Sriram Venkatapathy (Capital One), Varun Chandrasekaran (UIUC) and Gang Wang (UIUC) organized technical talks and working group sessions across three primary focus areas: Novel and diversity-driven red-teaming: Led by Capital One’s Sriram Venkatapathy, the session examined how financial AI systems must adhere to strict multilayered policy frameworks-spanning federal regulations (e.g., FCRA, UDAP), enterprise governance and application-specific constraints. Discussions highlighted that evaluating enterprise safety requires detecting policy omissions (such as missing mandatory disclosures or consent prompts) as well as defending against strategy-conditioned jailbreaks, chain-of-thought forgery and loopholes in complex policy specifications. Red-teaming multi-agent systems: Led by Gang Wang, this track focused on security vulnerabilities unique to multi-agent architectures. Researchers analyzed risks such as indirect prompt injection across workspace topologies, lateral attack propagation between trusted agents, execution-level coordination failures (e.g., data races and deadlocks) and communication-layer enforcement via protocols like NLIP. Evaluation of red-teaming and LLM judges: Led by Rikhiya Ghosh, participants tackled the open challenges of scientifically evaluating safety across long-horizon, multiturn interactions. The group audited LLM-as-a-judge frameworks using semantic factorization (MoE judges), probed reasoning traces for stealthy deception and monitorability failures and explored methods to prevent benchmark contamination through dynamic case generation. Fostering the frontier of talent and research The partnership between Capital One and UIUC continues to drive technical innovation while training the next generation of scientific talent. Highlighting joint breakthroughs like MEMGUARD-a defense mechanism preventing memory contamination in LLMs-the ASKS Center demonstrates the power of combining academic exploration with industrial scale. Capital One looks forward to continuing this strategic collaboration, advancing research in agentic AI and building systems that remain secure, trustworthy and beneficial at scale. title: FCA proposes greater pension investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers
raw_summary: Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected. The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates.Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.The FCA is clear that greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Providers should carefully weigh potential returns, risks and costs when making investment decisions, and any higher charges should be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.Alongside the proposed flexibility, the FCA is proposing safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees between savers and scrutiny of how private assets are valued. Providers and Independent Governance Committees would need access to the information necessary to assess whether performance-linked fees offer value for money.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said: 'People's pension savings should work hard for them. We want providers to have greater choice over how they invest for the long term where this can deliver better outcomes for savers.'But greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Any higher charges must be justified by additional value, with firms carefully weighing returns, risks and costs when deciding what is in savers' best interests.'The proposals would bring FCA rules more closely into line with the regime for trust-based pension schemes, where certain performance-linked fees have been excluded from the charge cap since 2023.Greater alignment would support competition and choice and reduce unnecessary complexity for providers operating across both parts of the market.The proposals would give providers an option, not an obligation, to use the exemption. Providers should do so only where it is in savers' interests, and they can meet the relevant protections.The FCA is seeking responses by 14 January 2027 and currently expects to make final rules in summer 2027 following consideration of feedback.Notes to editorsThe consultation is open until Thursday 14 January 2027. Read CP26/40: Exempting performance fees from the workplace pensions charge cap.This work is a priority under the FCA's Pensions Regulatory Priorities (PDF) and forms part of the wider pensions reform.In 2023, the Government changed the rules so certain performance fees sit outside the limit on charges, with protections for members. The proposals build on changes made for trust-based schemes in 2023, while reflecting developments in private markets and strengthening protections in areas such as how investments are valued.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA .

title: Man sentenced over £154m fake takeover bid targeting UK-listed company
raw_summary: Christopher Woolcott has today been given a 2-year prison sentence, suspended for 2 years, after staging a £154m fake takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration Inc. He was also ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and to pay costs of £4,627.73.Mr Woolcott built a sizeable stake in Touchstone, an oil and gas listed company. He then launched a bogus bid to drive up its share price. To give the bid credibility, Mr Woolcott invented several identities, forged takeover documents using Chat GPT and met Touchstone’s chief executive at a central London hotel under a false name. Touchstone ultimately determined that the bid was not legitimate.Had his plan succeeded, he stood to gain as much as £70,000 through the sale of his shares.The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) used a combination of its transaction reporting data, phone records, receipts, CCTV footage and evidence seized to identify Mr Woolcott as the person behind the fraud.Investigators traced three phone numbers used by different supposed individuals to contact Touchstone, to the same handset, and combined voter-register, open source research and FCA trading data to narrow down potential suspects. A parking payment also placed Mr Woolcott’s car near a Ryman store where the forged documents were sent from.Searches of Mr Woolcott's home and workplace later recovered the mobile phone linked to the fabricated identities, including a purported private equity partner, his supposed colleague and a fictitious solicitor.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'Mr Woolcott's fake takeover bid was a calculated attempt to profit by manipulating the market.'Our investigators followed an extensive evidence trail, exposed the fraud and identified the person behind the ruse.‘Anyone tempted to manipulate our markets should know that we are fully committed to identifying, investigating and taking action against those who seek to break the law.'In sentencing, Judge Karu said Mr Woolcott’s operation was deliberate, sophisticated, and planned in which four false identities and forged documents were used to hoodwink Touchstone Exploration Inc with a false takeover bid.Mr Woolcott pleaded guilty on 10 September 2026 to 1 count of fraud by false representation and 3 counts of making a false instrument.The investigation demonstrates how the FCA uses its full range of enforcement powers to disrupt financial crime and protect market integrity.The FCA opened its criminal investigation in March 2025, formally charged Mr Woolcott 16 months later and secured guilty pleas within 18 months of launching the case.Notes to editorsChristopher Woolcott, of Greenwich, London, was born on 23 April 1982.On 10 September 2026, Woolcott pleaded guilty at Westminster Magistrates’ Court to:1 count of fraud by false representation, contrary to sections 1 and 2 of the Fraud Act 2006; and3 counts of making a false instrument, contrary to sections 1 and 6 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981. Fraud by false representation is punishable by a fine and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment.Making a false instrument is punishable on indictment by a fine and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment.On 10 November 2026 at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Woolcott was sentenced to:a 2 year sentence, suspended for 2 years, and ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and pay costs of £4627.73; anda 14 months custodial sentence for each of the three forgery offences, to run concurrently with the two year suspended sentence.The FCA opened its criminal investigation in March 2025.Touchstone Exploration Inc is listed on AIM and the Toronto Stock Exchange. It was not under investigation by the FCA in connection with this case.Read the previous FCA press release: Man pleads guilty to fraud and forgery offences relating to fake takeover approach.Tackling market abuse and financial crime is a priority under the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

title: The not-so-fine print: making consumer contracts fair
raw_summary: How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders. When we take action We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use. Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to: Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; andIn some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA. Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress. Examples of cases we've tackledA crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.What we expect of firmsFirms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice. In practice, that means:Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to. Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to usConcerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.

title: FCA acts to protect consumers facing demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
raw_summary: We've intervened and Ethica Resolve Limited (Ethica), an FCA authorised firm that services and collects debt on behalf of creditors, has agreed to restrictions. These follow demands it made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. Ethica is acting on behalf of West 28th Street Limited (West 28), which bought disguised remuneration loans from a third party. West 28 is not authorised or regulated by the FCA.Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries. HMRC has published guidance for those affected.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they're unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Under the requirements we’ve agreed, Ethica:Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’. However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court. The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved. Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.
